abstract: The X-linked RNA helicase DDX3X is a high-risk gene for autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability primarily in females. Individuals with pathogenic variants in DDX3X have pervasive and often severe motor manifestations. Using mouse models, we studied the circuits underlying the motor phenotypes associated with Ddx3x deficiency and examined the feasibility of an early intervention to ameliorate motor trajectories. We show that Ddx3x controls both the development and later plasticity of motor circuits connecting the motor cortex with the pontine nuclei. Ddx3x haploinsufficiency during development affects the dendritic arborization of corticopontine neurons. Juvenile-onset Ddx3x loss in corticopontine neurons is sufficient to induce adult motor impairments overlapping with those caused by chemogenetic disruption of corticopontine circuits. Further, Ddx3x mutant mice engage corticopontine circuits in skilled motor tasks in a sex-dependent manner. Last, Ddx3x haploinsufficient female mice undergoing a juvenile motor intervention show long-lasting specific benefits in their adult motor function. Together, these findings establish Ddx3x as an essential regulator of corticopontine neuron development and function and provide an early motor intervention to ameliorate motor outcomes in a mouse model of DDX3X haploinsufficiency.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Ddx3x deficiency in mice impairs corticofugal motor circuits and causes motor deficits that are attenuated by early-life exercise

abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system's effective temperature with density.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating

abstract: Advances in nanoscale patterning of superconducting films [Y. L. Wang et al ., Nat. Nanotechnol. 13 , 560–565 (2018)] and the availability of submicron-sized superconducting single crystals with controlled geometry allow for the investigation of superconducting vortex matter under extreme confinement [A. K. Geim et al ., Nature 390 , 259–262 (1997)]. It has been observed in these systems that the interplay between sample geometry and vortex number results in the emergence of so-called “magic number” configurations which show unusually high stability against thermal fluctuations. However, a detailed, comprehensive theoretical study of the ground state and metastable states of confined vortex matter has not yet been developed. Here we show that the intricate properties of a system of vortices under extreme confinement can be characterized in detail by mapping the potential energy landscape of the system onto a network [J. P. K. Doye, Phys. Rev. Lett. 88 , 238701 (2002)] with nodes corresponding to local potential energy minima and edges to transition states between local minima. We apply these techniques to systems featuring repelling particles/vortices confined in small containers of various geometric shapes. We demonstrate that the ground state almost always belongs to a subset of system states within the deepest network core. We find that the emergence of magic number configurations in the ground state results in a drastic decrease in the complexity of the entire network. We use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to study the size dependence of melting in different configurations. We find that as confinement effects increase, magic number configurations transition to states with lower symmetry.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Potential energy landscape networks of confined vortex matter

abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor–regulated endothelial PD-L1

abstract: Natural selection enriches populations for genotypes that are well adapted to their environments, accumulating information about the selective conditions in the process. Therefore, selection can be viewed as a learning process through which populations acquire information about the environment. Motoo Kimura derived a relationship between the amount of information gained by selection and a measure of the inefficiency of the selective process, known as substitution load [M. Kimura, Genet. Res. 2, 127–140 (1961)]. Due to the gradual nature of selection and the ongoing mismatch of types to the environment, a lineage that is still acquiring information has lower mean fitness than a lineage that already has it. While this has been an influential insight, we find that Kimura’s model is inconsistent with selection experiments involving Escherichia coli . To address limitations in this model and develop a more robust measure for the efficiency of selection, we turn to computational learning theory. We show that the learning-theoretic concept of regret quantifies the inefficiency of selection as a learning process in terms of relative lineage fitness. We establish bounds on the efficiency of information gain in general settings, including frequency-dependent selection and arbitrary environmental change. We experimentally validate these bounds and demonstrate that our extended theory recovers Kimura’s fundamental insight. Finally, we show that selection is an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the basic problem faced by evolving populations and that it acquires information more efficiently than comparable processes in complex environments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The efficiency of information gain by natural selection

abstract: Clay minerals, ubiquitous across diverse geological systems, exert fundamental controls on critical geochemical processes, particularly through their adsorptive interactions with economically vital elements such as heavy rare earth elements (HREEs). The adsorption of HREEs onto clay surfaces is not only the key process that enriches these critical resources but also a potential archive for dating significant weathering events. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing the preferential adsorption and fractionation of rare earth elements (REEs) at mineral-water interfaces have remained poorly constrained. Here, employing in situ atomic-scale imaging via high-resolution atomic force microscopy, we systematically investigate the adsorption behaviors of light and heavy REEs (La, Y, Yb) onto key crystallographic planes-Si-basal, Al-basal, and edge terminations-of representative clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, mica) under environmentally relevant conditions (pH 4.8 to 6.4). We directly visualize and quantitatively reveal that Si-basal planes selectively enrich HREEs with pH-enhanced adsorption capacity, whereas Al-basal planes exhibit negligible REE adsorption below pH 5.8 but preferential HREE adsorption at pH 6.4. Integrating synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the adsorption mechanism of REE on Si-basal and Al-basal/edge planes as outer-sphere complexation and inner-sphere binding, respectively. Furthermore, we quantify the contributions of distinct planes via surface complexation modeling, revealing Si-dominated to Al- and edge-controlled adsorption with elevating pH. These atomic-scale findings not only resolve long-standing debates about clay mineral-mediated REE fractionation but also redefine fundamental paradigms of surface reactivity at silicate mineral-water interfaces, offering insights into the cycling and metallogeny of other critical metals in aqueous and sedimentary environments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Direct atomic-scale observation reveals rare earth element fractionation at mineral–water interfaces

abstract: We study a problem at the interface of enumerative algebraic geometry, algebraic combinatorics, and the statistical mechanics of vertex models with long-range interactions. We develop methods to explore the values S w ( 1 , … , 1 ) of Schubert polynomials (called principal specializations), which count reduced bumpless pipe dreams (RBPDs) with boundary permutation w ∈ S n . We exhibit counterexamples to the conjecture of Merzon and Smirnov that S w ( 1 n ) is maximized on layered permutations; the smallest such example we find is at n = 17. Despite the counterexamples, we present bounds that support a refined conjecture that the maximum of S w ( 1 n ) over all w ∈ S n grows at the same asymptotic rate as the maximum over layered permutations (found by Morales, Pak, and Panova). We implement and benchmark four recurrences for Schubert specializations: the descent formula of Macdonald, the transition formula of Lascoux–Schützenberger, the cotransition formula of Knutson, and the formula of Billey, Jockusch, and Stanley. We also explore typical random permutations drawn with probability proportional to S w ( 1 n ) , equivalently from uniformly random RBPDs. Our simulations reveal a permuton-like limit analogous to the Grothendieck setting studied by Morales, Panova, Petrov, and Yeliussizov. For sampling, we show that the standard monotone Coupling From The Past framework does not apply to RBPDs, leaving exact uniform sampling open. To bypass this, we develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler augmented with macroscopic “droop” updates that preserve connectivity and accelerate mixing. Our publicly available fast implementations reach n = 20 for exact computation of S w ( 1 n ) and n = 100 for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling using a chain whose stationary distribution is uniform on RBPDs (run on a cluster).
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Computation and sampling for Schubert specializations

abstract: The biological identity of nanoparticles is often redefined upon exposure to physiological fluids through the formation of a protein corona (PC), However, the molecular rules linking synthetic design to biological fate remain elusive owing to the fragmented and inconsistent proteomics data. Here, leveraging a standardized deep proteomic database of 42 diverse nanomaterials, we reveal the general molecular selection rules that govern the PC formation. We demonstrate that the PC is not a product of random adsorption but is shaped by strict property-dependent recruitment. First, surface charge regulates cellular uptake, with anionic nanoparticles specifically recruiting adhesion proteins to promote Itgav-mediated endocytosis, thus forming a causal charge-corona-receptor chain. Second, PEGylation engineers immune evasion by selectively depleting specific complement and coagulation factors, rather than merely preventing protein adsorption. Third, nanoparticle geometry imposes structural constraints and selects proteins based on specific physicochemical features such as lysine content. Beyond mechanistic insights, we show that material-specific PCs can rebalance the serum proteome and enable the detection of low-abundance disease biomarkers. This work shifts the paradigm from empirical description toward rule-based prediction and provides a foundational framework for rationally engineering nanomedicines with predictable and programmable biological identities.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Elucidating molecular regulatory rules of nanoparticle biological identity via standardized deep proteomics

abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85

abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons

abstract: Bioregionalization, the partitioning of the globe into areas of biotic similarity, is one of nature's most striking patterns, and highly congruent boundaries have been identified across plants, tetrapods, ants, and butterflies. However, these taxa also share a unimodal latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG), raising the question of whether bioregionalization and the LDG are mechanistically coupled or instead arise from largely independent processes acting on different timescales. Bees (Hymenoptera: Anthophila) provide a natural test, their diversity peaking at mid-latitudes rather than in the tropics. Using range estimates for 3,370 species and a phylogenetic beta-diversity framework, we recover 21 bee bioregions nested within at least six major realms (Australasia, Indomalaya-Oceania, Nearctic, Neotropics, Palearctic, and Sub-Sahara) that closely align with those of other taxa despite bees' atypical diversity gradient. We propose that bioregionalization and species richness are decoupled because they arise from distinct processes: the former reflects historical dispersal and evolutionary history, the latter local diversification, extinction, and environmental filtering. Our analysis provides a global biogeographic framework for future bee research and highlights the processes shaping the world's major biogeographic boundaries.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Global bee bioregions mirror those of other taxa despite a uniquely bimodal latitudinal diversity gradient

abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont's electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes

abstract: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine-Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol-Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth's deep water cycle.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Hydration at the base of the mantle transition zone by ancient subductions in Asia

abstract: We address the inverse problem for complexity functions of infinite words, which asks which functions can occur as complexity functions of infinite words. We survey our recent advances on this problem and several of its ramifications. We describe an asymptotic solution to the inverse problem, realizing every function satisfying two necessary conditions as the complexity function of an infinite word up to asymptotic equivalence. We then turn to phenomena beyond asymptotic equivalence, presenting constructions of infinite words with seemingly contradictory behavior of the discrete derivatives of their complexity functions. These lead to a solution of a 1995 problem of Cassaigne and to applications in symbolic dynamics, including the question of convergence of Rauzy graphs, as well as to the growth and asymptotic invariants of algebraic structures.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Complexity functions of infinite sequences

abstract: Monolayers of group-VI transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are two-dimensional semiconductors that exhibit exceptionally strong light-matter coupling yet typically suffer from low emission quantum yields. In this letter, we investigate the heavily n-doped regime of a WSe$_2$ monolayer and show that multi-particle excitonic complexes produce photoluminescence signals up to two orders of magnitude stronger than in the neutral state. Time-resolved photoluminescence and differential reflectivity measurements reveal that the quantum yield rises with carrier density and exceeds 50% for electron concentrations above 10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$. These findings establish TMD monolayers as a platform for exploring excitonic complexes in high-density electron gases and point toward new opportunities for efficient, atomically thin light emitters.
title: High luminescence efficiency of multivalley excitonic complexes in heavily doped WSe 2 monolayer

abstract: Low-entropy motional states of ion Coulomb crystals are an essential prerequisite for a plethora of applications and are typically prepared by laser cooling. As larger crystals are operated in the quantum regime, it remains unclear, and has recently become debated, whether increasing the ion number can be beneficial for cooling. Here, we investigate theoretically and experimentally many-ion sideband cooling and the role of collective effects in different spin-motion coupling regimes. For weak coupling, the many-body effects are insignificant. In the strong-coupling regime, however, the spin and motional subsystems undergo a coherent state swap, enabling cooling by a suitably timed laser pulse. Using planar Coulomb crystals with up to 91 ions, we demonstrate that the residual mean phonon occupation after one such pulse scales as $1/N^2$ with the number of ions. By iterating the pulses, we measure mean phonon occupations $<2\cdot10^{-4}$. For large crystals in the coherent regime, we further show that the spin-motion dynamics becomes largely independent of the initial phonon statistics. Through spin measurements, the state-swap mechanism can be utilized to probe the phonon distribution in the mode.
title: Collective enhancement in sideband cooling of ion crystals

abstract: We show that the conformal anomaly of a $(1+1)$-dimensional conformal field theory can be extracted directly from a ground-state wave-function overlap associated with a spatial conformal deformation. Focusing on the $q$-Möbius deformation, we derive an exact overlap formula between the deformed and undeformed ground states, whose exponent directly encodes the central charge. Motivated by this result, we construct a lattice estimator based solely on ground-state overlaps and apply it to representative critical quantum chains and the gapless edge modes of a two-dimensional Chern insulator. Numerical results demonstrate that the resulting overlaps provide a simple and robust probe of the central charge in microscopic models. We further demonstrate that the deformed ground states retain universal geometric structures in their entanglement spectra and entanglement entropies. These results provide a simple wave-function-based route to probing conformal data in critical systems and topological edge modes.
title: Extracting central charge from ground-state overlaps of spatially deformed Hamiltonians

abstract: Shot noise has been used to measure fractional charges of anyons. The value of the charge imposes constraints on fractional statistics but does not determine it. This issue is particularly important in multi-component systems. For example, the zero charge of neutral anyons in bilayer graphene gives no information about their statistics at all. We propose a protocol to probe the statistics of charged and neutral anyons in multi-component systems with layer-resolved or spin-resolved noise. The protocol applies to the fractional quantum spin Hall effect in MoTe$_2$, topological states in multi-layer graphene and bilayer GaAs, and to recently discovered fractional excitons in bilayer graphene. The approach relies on the relation between statistics and the distribution of the anyon charge over the components. Information about statistics can also be extracted from a simpler measurement of the layer-resolved electric current through a narrow constriction in a Hall bar even in the presence of long-range interactions and other non-universal effects.
title: Probing bilayer topological order with layer-resolved transport

abstract: We present the first implementation of a novel extension of the Generator Coordinate Method (GCM), dubbed the enhanced GCM (eGCM), which is applied to the grazing Multi-Nucleon Transfer (MNT) reaction $^{48}$Ca+$^{208}$Pb near the Coulomb barrier. eGCM incorporates major qualitative differences with either Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) or GCM frameworks used until now for nuclear reactions. We demonstrate that the eGCM framework describes for the first time in a fully quantum microscopic framework the emergence and the time-evolution of Niels Bohr's 1936 conjectured Compound Nucleus (CN). The thermalization time extracted in eGCM is at least two orders of magnitude larger than the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) would predict.
title: Multi-nucleon transfer reactions and the emergence and the evolution of the compound nucleus

abstract: We present a scheme for implementing a high-fidelity non-linear phase shift on a photonic state. The scheme is based on repeated scattering off a two-level quantum emitter embedded in a chiral or one-sided waveguide. The waveguide is equipped with elements inducing second-order dispersion and temporal phase shifts, which effectively form a harmonic trap and confine the photon pulses to a Gaussian shape. The same quantum emitter can be used for each scattering, and thus, only one quantum emitter is needed in this scheme. To illustrate the application of our scheme for photonic quantum computing and quantum communication, we analyze the implementation of a control-Z gate and a deterministic Bell-state analyzer for photonic qubits. Through numerical optimization, we show that we can reach a control-Z gate fidelity of $\mathcal{F} \sim 99.2\%$ ($\mathcal{F} \sim 96\%$) and a success probability of $P_s \sim 99.6 \%$ ($P_s\sim 98 \%$) for a Bell-state measurement with $N=17$ ($N=5$) scatterings.
title: High fidelity photon-photon gates by scattering off a two-level quantum emitter

abstract: Development of a $^{229}$Th nuclear optical clock requires precise and model-insensitive nuclear-structure parameters, which presently suffer from limited accuracy and poor consistency. We propose a joint spectroscopy scheme using two highly charged $^{229}$Th ions with $J=1/2$ electronic ground states, where the lowest electronic excitation energy of each ion far exceeds the nuclear transition energy. This configuration effectively forms a three-level system comprising the electronic ground state and the nuclear ground ($g$) and isomeric ($m$) states, resulting in strongly enhanced nuclear hyperfine mixing. Within this framework, a unified analysis of precision measurements on both ions enables the simultaneous determination of five key nuclear parameters without relying on external nuclear inputs: the magnetic dipole moments $μ_g$ and $μ_m$, the bare-nucleus transition energy $ω_n$, the charge-radius difference $δ\langle r^{2}\rangle_{gm}$, and the $M1$ transition matrix element $T_{M1}$. With this approach, the uncertainties in $ω_n$ and $δ\langle r^{2}\rangle_{gm}$ are estimated to be reduced by factors of 3 and 2, respectively, relative to their current uncertainties. %compared with current values. This work could provide a useful benchmark for nuclear theory and serve as a foundation for future development of a $^{229}$Th-based nuclear optical clock.
title: Simultaneous determination of multiple nuclear parameters of 229 Th using highly charged ions

abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. By analyzing global corpora consisting of 367 bird species (>74,500 vocal elements from ~5900 songs) within two clades of vocal learners (oscines and hummingbirds) and related nonlearners (suboscines and nightjars) and 52 human languages (>15,000 elements in >800 speech or song phrases), we revealed common patterns in bird songs that resemble prevalent patterns in human speech and song with variation in resemblance to speech or song. Vocal learning did not systematically affect acoustic patterning or similarity to human vocalizations. These data underscore the deep analogies between bird and human vocalizations and convergent motor mechanisms shaping communication.
title: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning

abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Here we provide direct experimental evidence for a chiral magnon in the altermagnetic candidate manganese telluride (MnTe) revealed by circular-dichroism resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. This mode, which we term chiral altermagnon, exhibits a distinct momentum dependence of its spin polarization consistent with the altermagnetic g -wave symmetry of MnTe. Our polarization-resolved data corroborate the existence of a discrete class of magnetic excitations, demonstrating how altermagnetic order shapes spin dynamics and paving the way for advances in spintronic and quantum technologies.
title: Chiral altermagnon in MnTe

abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. We report the observation of a Chern metal at the onset of the magnetic Kondo breakdown in a frustrated moiré Kondo lattice--angle-aligned MoTe 2 /WSe 2 bilayers. The state is compressible and is manifested by a nearly quantized Hall resistance and a finite longitudinal resistance arising from a bad metallic bulk. We demonstrate the presence of a chiral edge state by nonlocal transport measurements and current-induced quantum anomalous Hall breakdown. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements further reveal a magnetization plateau for the Chern metal before a metamagnetic transition at the Kondo breakdown. Our results open an opportunity for moiré engineering of exotic quantum phases through the interplay between band topology and Kondo interactions.
title: Emergence of Chern metal in a moiré Kondo lattice

abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Consistent use of the Sun compass relies on the endogenous clock to track the Sun’s arc, yet animals traveling east-west experience time shifts, potentially causing mismatches between their internal clock and local time. Using GPS, we reveal that Manx shearwaters ( Puffinus puffinus ) experience such shifts during homing flights, generating predictable errors in Sun compass orientation. Use of the Sun compass persists even when shearwaters have access to compass-independent cues during coast following. Our findings provide a new avenue for chronobiology research in the wild, suggesting that rapid longitudinal movements may affect other processes governed by the endogenous clock and that conserved chronobiological mechanisms impose substantial constraints on navigation.
title: Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and Sun compass error

abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Mars’ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks. We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites. We determine that Teg 001 is a sample of ancient crust, which formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18 O, before ejection into space by an impact.
title: A Martian meteorite that formed ≳4.1 billion years ago samples Mars’ early crust and mantle

abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.
title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity

abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development-its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.
title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth

abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.
title: Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF 2

abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.
title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival

abstract: The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium-derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. Finally, we delineate three transcriptionally distinct steroidogenic lineages differing in cholesterol sourcing, cortisol synthesis, and sex hormone production that together orchestrate sex differentiation. These findings deepen our understanding of urogenital system assembly and guide the exploration of coordinated multiorgan development.
title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis

abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.
title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness

abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension-the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as "Least Concern" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.
title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm

abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.
title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting

abstract: A complete cell type transcriptome atlas of a vertebrate could promote understanding of animal cell type composition, organization, and evolution. The miniaturized, transparent, and regenerative teleost Danionella cerebrum brings whole-vertebrate single-cell profiling experiments within reach. We performed region-stratified single-cell RNA sequencing across the adult Danionella body and mapped cell types and gene expression at single-cell resolution using spatial transcriptomics. We delineated spatially distinct neural cell types on the basis of their regional gene expression signatures. The body-wide atlas elucidated cell types harboring adult molecular positional memory, uncovered paedomorphic features, and revealed conserved body-region and appendage-specification programs in adult connective tissue. Comparative analyses revealed conserved neural cell types, and regeneration datasets uncovered expression dynamics during telencephalon regeneration. This whole-vertebrate transcriptome atlas yields a comprehensive resource for myriad questions in biology and neuroscience.
title: Whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate, Danionella cerebrum

abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) prevents self-fertilization through highly polymorphic genetic recognition at the S locus with multiple alleles. In Papaver rhoeas , the S determinants were previously identified as PrpS and PrsS . However, we found that PrpS-PrsS was absent in many S haplotypes. In this work, we report the identification of an alternative pair of polymorphic S genes, S locus oligopeptide transporter ( SOPT ) and S locus glycine-rich protein ( SGRP ), segregating at the S locus when PrpS-PrsS is absent. SOPT and SGRP display hallmark S determinant features and confer SI when heterologously expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana . Therefore, instead of having allelomorphs with homologous variants, the Papaver SI system is determined by two multiallelic idiomorphs sharing no obvious common ancestry. This discovery of a dual-idiomorph system reveals a distinct genetic basis for polymorphism, with implications for the evolution of allorecognition mechanisms.
title: Papaver self-incompatibility is controlled by two multiallelic idiomorphs

abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning-assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth-based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.
title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes

abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.
title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
